title: I. W. Bernheim, from peddler to I. W. Harper
summary: Isaac W. Bernheim landed in New York in 1867 with about four dollars, peddled in Pennsylvania until his horse died, built Bernheim Brothers and the I. W. Harper label in Paducah and Louisville, and gave Kentucky Bernheim Forest.
bodyMarkdown:
[Isaac Wolfe Bernheim](/people/#isaac-w-bernheim) landed at [Castle Garden](https://grokipedia.com/page/Castle_Clinton), New York's immigrant station, at noon on April 8, 1867. Asked how much money he carried, he told the commissioner: a few small coins and [twenty francs in gold](https://archive.org/details/TheStoryOfTheBernheimFamily), "about four dollars in American money." He was eighteen, born on November 4, 1848, in Schmieheim, a small village in the Grand Duchy of Baden.

## A peddler's pack

His uncle had no work for him. An old schoolmate of the uncle, John Weil of Wilkes-Barre, suggested that the boy peddle, so the uncle bought him, on credit, a box of "Yankee notions": needles, pins, spool thread, socks, suspenders, handkerchiefs and stockings. On May 3, 1867, Bernheim left for Pennsylvania.

By October he had saved enough for a horse and wagon. When winter came he opened a little store at Overton, a Pennsylvania crossroads, and left the lame horse with a farmer named Stroh. In the spring his uncles, giving up in New York, offered him a clerk's place in their old home of [Paducah](/stories/paducah-at-the-tennessee-mouth/).

He was about to refuse when a letter from Stroh reported the horse dead. "Pennsylvania thereby lost a peddler," he wrote; "Kentucky gained a young clerk."

## Bernheim Brothers of Paducah

In Paducah he became bookkeeper for the wholesale liquor house of [Loeb, Bloom & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Wolfe_Bernheim) and saved enough to bring over his brother Bernard. The brothers had less than $1,200 between them, so a grocer named Elbridge Palmer put in a couple of thousand dollars as silent partner. Bernheim Brothers opened on January 1, 1872, in the back part of Palmer's store on Market Street.

At first they sold within about two hundred miles of Paducah; within fifteen years their trade covered the whole South and reached into the West. Their best-known label was [I. W. Harper](https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/i-w-harper-a-comprehensive-collectors-guide), first marketed in 1879. The initials were Isaac's own. Where "Harper" came from is not clearly recorded.

## Main Street, Louisville

On April 1, 1888, the firm moved to Louisville, then one of the great distributing centers for fine whiskies, and took a building on Main Street between First and Second. In March 1896 fire destroyed the bonded warehouses at a Pleasure Ridge Park distillery the firm owned with partners, and the government held Bernheim to the tax bond on the burned whiskey. He fought for nearly eighteen months before Treasury Secretary Lyman J. Gage cancelled the bond on the day before Thanksgiving, 1897.

Meanwhile the brothers built a distillery of their own near the city limits on the Illinois Central Railroad. The first mash ran in April 1897. In 1899 Bernheim offered Louisville a bronze Thomas Jefferson by the sculptor Moses Ezekiel; it [stands at the Jefferson County courthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Wolfe_Bernheim).

## Kentucky today

In 1928 Bernheim bought Bullitt County land that had been [stripped for iron ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernheim_Arboretum_and_Research_Forest), paying about a dollar an acre. He founded Bernheim Forest in 1929 and gave it in trust to the people of Kentucky. The Olmsted firm began designing it in 1931, and it opened in 1950, five years after his death on April 1, 1945.

He and his first wife, Amanda, are buried there. The forest near Clermont now covers more than 16,000 acres. Our Bourbon Series also tells of [George Garvin Brown](/stories/george-garvin-brown-and-old-forester/) and [Frederick Stitzel](/stories/frederick-stitzels-barrel-racks-1879/). The map pins mark Paducah, the Main Street block in Louisville and the forest.
